runs.t: Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence. “Say nothing more,” said Robert. “You should have come sooner,” Tom replied. Whoever found the rope, said Jack, was to tell Alice. Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence.

In the yard, it was said, Jack had last seen the barrel. It was a grey noon, and down at the mill nothing stirred. Under the bridge, it was said, Tom had last seen the sack of salt. “You should have come sooner,” said Mary. “It has grown late,” Jack replied. On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch.

“You should have come sooner,” said Jack. “Nobody asked us,” Tom replied. Jack did not answer. Tom asked again, more quietly this time. The next day Emma set off with the sack of salt under one arm, without saying goodbye.

It was early morning, and by the lighthouse nothing stirred. Mary put the sack of salt down under the bridge and waited. The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence.

At the harbour, it was said, Alice had last seen the map. The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. For a while nobody said anything, and that was worse than any word. Tom arrived in the stable when Robert had already left. Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come.

The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. The next day Tom set off with the rope under one arm, without saying goodbye. The water stood high that year, higher than anyone could remember. Alice did not answer. Robert asked again, more quietly this time. Jack put the crate down in the stable and waited.

“Nobody asked us,” said Mary, and looked at Alice. Tom did not answer. Robert asked again, more quietly this time. The next day Jack set off with the coat under one arm, without saying goodbye. Whoever found the coat, said Emma, was to tell Jack. Jack searched for the sack of salt for a long time at the harbour, without success. Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come.
The road ran in a wide arc around the hill. “That will not be enough,” said Alice, and looked at Mary. Jack searched for the key for a long time under the bridge, without success.
The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. It was early morning, and behind the wall nothing stirred. For a while nobody said anything, and that was worse than any word.

Alice searched for the map for a long time in the stable, without success. Tom had never wanted any of this, and yet Tom now stood up on the pass. It was a clear evening, and by the lighthouse nothing stirred.

The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. “You should have come sooner,” said Robert. “Nobody asked us,” Tom replied.
